extractions.value: Our patient fulfills the clinical and electrophysiological criteria of Lorish and colleagues [1] for SMS. The patient had high titers of anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies in both serum and cerebrospinal fluid. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of brain and spinal cord was normal. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) revealed a distinctive motor evoked potential (MEP) pattern in proximal lower limb muscles consisting of markedly increased MEP amplitudes and MEP/M ratios, reduced excitability thresholds, and absent silent period. Treatment with benzodiazepine and baclofen normalized both the clinical picture and the MEP values.

There was marked improvement. Stiffness and spasms disappeared, CMUA was not detected in EMG examination and LLR responses could not be elicited at rest. All MEP values normalized except for VM SP duration (Table 1). The patient became able to walk outdoors and on uneven ground and to return to work without limitations in activities of daily living. Over a 3-year follow-up she remained stable on neurologic and EMG examinations and TMS persisted normally except for reduced VM SP duration (Table 1).

A dose of 9 mg/day bromazepam in three divided doses reduced stiffness and spasms. Higher doses were not tolerated because of somnolence. Equivalent doses of diazepam were also effective. We gradually added tizanidine to bromazepam up to a daily dose of 18 mg. This further improved stiffness and spasms and the patient could walk unassisted. Tizanidine was discontinued and baclofen was gradually added to bromazepam up to 75 mg/day in three divided doses. There was marked improvement.
Because of the benign course, immunosuppressive therapy was not carried out.
